tooth and nail phrase

also fight tooth and nail, with might and main, doggedly, with the teeth, with all one’s might, with hands and feet

classical

Cic. Tusc. 2.56 (Lewis & Short s.v. ungula)
Traupman 109: tōtō corpore et omnibus ungulīs
Traupman 396

tōtō corpore atque omnibus ungulīs

ablatives of means

with tooth and nail, with might and main

Literally “with the whole body and all the claws”: Latin fights with hooves and talons where English has teeth and nails.

Other words

  • mordicus — with the teeth; and so holding on for all one is worth

    adverb · also used · classical · Plaut. Curc. 597: manum arripuit mordicus; Cic. Ac. 2.51: rem mordicus tenēre (Lewis & Short)

    From mordeō. Mordicus tenēre, to hold fast to a thing and not give it up.

  • manibus pedibus — with hands and feet: with all one’s might

    also used · classical · Ter. And. 676: cōnārī manibus pedibus noctēsque et diēs; Ter. And. 161: manibus pedibus obnīxē omnia factūrum

    (vōx cōmica: Ter.)

    Lewis & Short s.v. manus gives it as manibus pedibusque, “with might and main”; Terence has the two words without -que.

Examples

  • ut eum ēriperet, manum arripuit mordicus

    to snatch it away, she seized my hand with her teethPlaut. Curc. 597

  • cōnārī manibus pedibus noctēsque et diēs

    to strive with hand and foot, night and dayTer. And. 676
